claims.text: PACELC, a classic extension of the CAP theorem: if there is a partition (P), a system chooses availability (A) or consistency (C); else (E), it chooses lower latency (L) or consistency (C).
claims.source_hint: The PACELC formulation (extension of CAP); outline item 1; DECISIONS 2026-10-22 (8): classic reference, no name, no year

claims.text: Latency is the time from sending a request to receiving its answer.

Without any failure, the owner of the data takes a write first and other copies learn of it afterwards, so keeping copies in step costs time: a read from a nearby copy is fast but may be old, a write that waits until the copies it names have it answers later.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 2; PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.5 Streaming Replication (small delay between commit on primary and visibility on standby)

claims.text: A read from the owner (the primary database) sees the latest committed value; viewing your own order reads PostgreSQL, so an order you just placed is always there.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 13.2.1 Read Committed (a statement sees data committed before it began); docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md @ stage-4 line 17

claims.text: Fast and current are not two goals a design simply meets together: the time a copy needs to catch up is paid either by the caller, who waits, or by the data, which may be old.
ProductCache.FindAsync returns the Redis copy on a cache hit without querying PostgreSQL (line 29); the TTL is 5 minutes (line 18); a missed delete leaves the old copy until the TTL ends (line 17).
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Catalog/ProductCache.cs @ stage-4 lines 16-29, 85-96 (SetAsync with Ttl); StackExchange.Redis StringSetAsync expiry

claims.text: UpdatePriceAsync (outside the excerpt) deletes the Redis copy after the price is saved, so the next read loads the new price.

The order price also goes through ProductCache; consistency-per-operation.md records that an order placed while a stale copy lives uses the old price, which the team accepts, and that if a shop needs a price change to apply to orders at once, placing an order must read the primary.

PostgreSQL replication (the stream of changes db-replica receives) is asynchronous by default: db commits and answers without waiting for the replica, so the replica can be behind (also stated in Before you start).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.5 Streaming Replication ('asynchronous by default'); 19.6.2 synchronous_standby_names (empty = no synchronous replication)

claims.text: replica-lag.sh: after the UPDATE returns on db, db returns 1300000 and db-replica still returns 1250000; 6 seconds later db-replica returns 1300000.
The lab replica waits 5 seconds before applying each committed change, set in db/replica/start.sh (recovery_min_apply_delay=5s), so the stale read shows on every run.
claims.source_hint: db/replica/start.sh @ stage-4 lines 15-18; PostgreSQL 17 docs 19.6.4 recovery_min_apply_delay

claims.text: With synchronous replication each commit waits until a standby db is configured to wait for confirms it has the change, so writes answer later and the standby holds each change committed this way. A standby receives a change before applying it; reads show only applied changes.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.8; 19.5.1 synchronous_commit (remote_apply = replayed, visible to queries); replica-lag.sh @ stage-4 lines 34-35 (receives at once, applies after 5 s)

claims.text: The api has one connection string (ConnectionStrings:Default, naming its database server), pointing at the primary; the product list may move to db-replica, viewing your own order and a ProductCache read may not (a reload from a lagging replica restores the old price for a TTL).
claims.source_hint: docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md @ stage-4 lines 38-53 and table lines 13-17; outline items 5-6

claims.text: With asynchronous replication, if the primary's data is lost, commits not yet copied to the replica may be lost with it; a change the replica already holds survives.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.5 Streaming Replication / 26.2.8 ('if the primary server crashes then some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby, causing data loss')

claims.text: If no synchronous standby can be reached, commits on the primary wait until one becomes available.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.8.4 Planning for High Availability (commits wait when synchronous standbys are unavailable)

claims.text: Read a nearby copy when an old value harms nobody; read the owner when the caller must see the latest value; use synchronous replication when a committed change must survive losing the primary; keep asynchronous for the product list, whose row already accepts old data.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md @ stage-4 table and lines 38-53; outline items 2, 4, 5

claims.text: A cache is a copy, so it is a consistency choice: ProductCache answers without asking PostgreSQL, so its answer can be as old as its TTL allows.

Design table, normal running: one product chooses low latency (ProductCache); the product list and viewing your own order read the primary, the list only because no other copy exists yet; read-your-writes also rules out keeping orders in Redis.

beyond_scope: One clause: synchronous commit waits for the standby to hold the change, not necessarily to show it to reads (setting not named), to keep 'holds every committed change' exact
